title: Fission surface power for lunar and Martian outposts
bottleneck: A sustained Moon or Mars base needs tens to hundreds of kilowatts of continuous power — through the 14-day lunar night and global Martian dust storms that cripple solar. Fission surface power (Kilopower demonstrated ~10 kW) is the leading answer, but scaling up means autonomous reactor operation, regolith-shielded emplacement, heat rejection, and a launch-and-landing architecture for a fueled reactor that has never flown. Regulatory approval for launching an active nuclear payload adds years.
why_it_blocks: Without reliable night-and-storm power, ISRU plants cannot run, habitats cannot stay warm, and a base reverts to short solar-powered sorties instead of permanent presence.
current_state: Kilopower's KRUSTY test (2018) proved the concept at small scale; NASA and DOE are working toward a ~40 kW lunar fission surface power demo targeted for the early 2030s. No flight unit exists.
